Liberals say it’s quite extraordinary the government has put its hand up to co-host the UN climate summit in Turkey, and has failed to secure an agreement between nations.
The EU, UK and some allies rejected the deal on the future of the climate which didn’t even mention fossil fuels.
Deputy Liberal leader says the country should be concerned we couldn’t broker a deal. Jane Hume told News24:
It’s pretty extraordinary, isn’t it? We’ve spent $150 million to get Chris Bowen to COP, to host COP. Then we found out it was actually a co-host deal. Now we’re walking away without a deal at all. This is quite extraordinary.
It hasn’t been, since 2009, when Kevin Rudd was in Copenhagen, that we had no agreement, but to have no deal at all, this is quite exceptional, and I think it should be something that Australia should be concerned about.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting week of the year! (Don’t sound too excited.)
It’s crunch time for Labor who have several key pieces of legislation they want to pass this week including digital duty of care, the gas reservation scheme, changes to capital gains tax for trusts, and reducing private health insurance premiums for over 65s.
So far they’re closer to a deal on the first two, trusts is somewhere in between, and private health is looking iffy – but anything is possible.
Labor is also going to cop some heat (get it!) after climate talks broke down at the UN Cop summit where the energy minister, Chris Bowen, was the chief negotiator.
I’ve got my coffee, I hope you’ve got yours – let’s get stuck in.
Albanese trails Angus Taylor as preferred PM in Newspoll
AnthonyAlbanese returns from a series of overseas summits to crunch negotiations on multiple proposed changes as his popularity takes a further nosedive, as Australian Associated Press reports.
The Labor leader trails his opposition counterpart, AngusTaylor, as preferred prime minister for the first time, according to a Newspoll published in The Australian on Monday.
Albanese’s net approval rating also hit a new low of minus 31, while the Coalition managed to claw back some voter support. Its primary vote stood at 22% in the latest survey, behind One Nation and Labor, which were tied on 27%.
Wong warns about AI in major foreign policy speech
AI is a foreign policy and national security challenge, Penny Wong will tell parliament this week, raising concerns in a major speech about how the growing technology is being used in war and foreign interference.
Wong will give a substantial foreign policy address to parliament on Tuesday, with advance speech notes detailing a focus on artificial intelligence. The foreign affairs minister will warn that AI tools “make that [foreign] interference faster, cheaper and harder to recognise”.
Wong says Australia welcomes investment in AI but urged a focus on safety - particularly on the international stage.
We must do what we can to ensure that the race to develop frontier AI, concentrated in a handful of companies and countries, does not reward speed over prudence.
Australia has helped shape the international order before, in non-proliferation and in online safety. With artificial intelligence, we intend to do it again.
AnikaWells said the government would consult on how to exempt low-risk small businesses – and potentially other services – from the digital duty of care legislation before it comes into effect 12 months later.
Business groups had called for such a change but the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry had urged that it be specifically included in the legislation, not worked out later via regulation. Its chief executive, AndrewMcKellar, said:
A small business should not have to engage lawyers simply to work out whether its website is caught by a regime carrying penalties of more than $100m. The answer should be in black and white in the legislation.
The Greens are expected to eventually back the bill but more negotiations will continue this week.
Small business carveout for digital duty of care legislation
Josh Butler
Labor will exempt small businesses from its digital duty of care legislation – a key request from business groups, and potentially another step toward getting the bill passed.
The government is still seeking the support of the Greens on the bill, who want tougher penalties.
The carveout for small businesses from new regulations was not at the top of the Greens’ agenda – they also want a new ombudsman for big tech – but the new update from the communications minister, AnikaWells, shows Labor is in the mood to make deals.
She said:
The intention of the digital duty of care is to put the onus on tech companies to protect Australians from online harms before they occur – not to create additional burden for low-risk small businesses.
A low-risk website for a cafe or bookkeeper is unlikely to cause harm to its users so, once the digital duty of care starts, they will be exempt from the law. We will work closely with small business to get the setting right.
digest_he: הממשלה באוסטרליה עומדת בפני שבוע מכריע בפרלמנט שכולל קידום חקיקה בנושא חובת זהירות דיגיטלית, תוך מתן פטור לעסקים קטנים בסיכון נמוך כדי לרצות את ארגוני העסקים. במקביל, שר האקלים כריס בואן ספג ביקורת קשה לאחר שפסגת האקלים של האו
